title: Saqqara & Dahshur: Are They Worth Visiting?
excerpt: Are Saqqara and Dahshur worth visiting? Yes, if Giza is on your list: Djoser's Step Pyramid, the Bent and Red pyramids and Memphis on a 9-hour loop from €33.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

Quick answer

Yes, if Giza is already on your list. Saqqara is where the pyramid was invented (Djoser's Step Pyramid, the first large stone building anyone raised), Dahshur is where it was perfected (Sneferu's Bent and Red pyramids), and both sit on one quiet desert loop south of Cairo that usually takes in Memphis, Egypt's ancient capital, on the way. One long day, about 9 hours door to door, from €33 per person, as listed in November 2026.

UNESCO describes the pyramid fields from Giza to Dahshur as one World Heritage site.

Giza casts a long shadow: most Cairo itineraries book it as the pyramid day and stop there. South of the city, though, stand the pyramids that came first and the experiments that made Giza possible, in fields where you can hear the wind instead of the tour buses. This guide answers the question a Cairo planner actually asks: are Saqqara and Dahshur worth a second pyramid day, and is Memphis more than a box to tick? It is written by the team behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure marketplace. We have worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993, and this trio is a day tour in our catalogue.

The short answer: yes, if you have a second pyramid day in you

Saqqara and Dahshur are worth visiting in three specific situations, and honestly not worth forcing outside them.

  • You want the full pyramid story. Giza shows the finished article. Saqqara shows the prototype, Djoser's Step Pyramid, and Dahshur shows the failed draft and the fix. Together they explain why Giza looks the way it does.
  • You want pyramid scale without the crowds. Giza is Egypt's best-known pyramid site and the busiest. Djoser's enclosure and Dahshur's open desert are markedly quieter.
  • You want to walk into a pyramid. At Dahshur, the Red Pyramid's interior is covered by the site ticket, with no supplement, unlike Giza, where the pyramid interiors are separately ticketed. On the tour, your guide advises on the day.

The honest counterweight: if Cairo has given you exactly one day, spend it at Giza. Midsummer afternoons are punishing on exposed desert plateau, and Saqqara involves genuine walking on uneven ground, so travellers with limited mobility should plan around it.

Saqqara: where the pyramid was invented

Saqqara's claim is simple and enormous: the Step Pyramid of Djoser, built around 2670 BC, is the first large stone building anyone raised. The architect Imhotep stacked ever-smaller mastabas, the flat tomb rectangles of the era, into a staircase to the sky. The pyramid stands inside a vast limestone enclosure whose ceremonial courts have been restored.

The Step Pyramid is the headline, but Saqqara is a whole necropolis. Around the enclosure sit the mastabas of nobles, their walls carved with scenes of farming, fishing and feasting. The Serapeum holds the granite vaults where the sacred Apis bulls were buried; it is sold on its own ticket (EGP 340 on the Ministry list) and is not included on the Sawa tour. The Imhotep Museum, covered by the main Saqqara ticket, makes sense of what you have walked through. New discoveries are still announced here regularly: Saqqara is an active excavation, not a finished museum. On a one-day loop there is time for the Step Pyramid enclosure and one or two highlights. Dedicated explorers give it half a day.

The texture is the selling point: sand underfoot, stone paths, and the Step Pyramid's silhouette against the desert with no coach park in the frame.

Dahshur: the pyramid's failed draft and its fix

Dahshur is where Sneferu, Khufu's father, learned how to build a true pyramid, and his two pyramids here tell the story in stone. The Bent Pyramid starts steep, at about 54 degrees, and visibly changes angle partway up, to about 43 degrees. The usual explanation is that the builders corrected course mid-build when the structure showed signs of strain, leaving Egypt's strangest silhouette. It is the rare great pyramid that still carries much of its original smooth casing.

The Red Pyramid, a short drive away, is the payoff: the first true, smooth-sided pyramid completed successfully. You climb a flight of steps up its north face and descend a long, steep, low passage to chambers with high corbelled ceilings. The interior is covered by the Dahshur site ticket, and on the tour your guide advises on the day. Low ceilings and bent passages mean you should skip it if you are claustrophobic or unsteady on stairs, and the chambers themselves are bare: the scale of the pyramid against the empty desert is the real sight. The Bent Pyramid's interior reopened to visitors in 2019, for the first time since 1965, but interiors can close for conservation, so treat access as something to confirm on the day.

Stand at the Red Pyramid's base and you are looking at the draft Khufu improved on one generation later at Giza. That is the whole reason this day pairs so well with a Giza morning.

Memphis: the old capital, and whether to add it

Memphis, at the village of Mit Rahina, was Egypt's capital for centuries after its founding, traditionally by King Menes around 5,000 years ago. Almost nothing of the city stands above ground. What visitors see is a small open-air museum built around two survivors: the reclining limestone Colossus of Ramesses II, laid out in a viewing hall so you can walk its length at eye level, and the Alabaster Sphinx, carved from a single block.

As a destination on its own, Memphis is thin: a short visit of an hour or so is usual. As part of this loop it works. It sits on the route, its "capital before the pyramids" story sets up the day, and it breaks the drive from Cairo. If you want the sequel, another colossus of Ramesses II, in granite, now greets visitors in the entrance atrium of the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza.

How the day runs: the 9-hour shape and what it costs

The day trip runs the three stops in one loop with lunch in the middle, about 9 hours in all. Hotel pickup is included. The order on the Sawa listing:

  1. Drive south to Memphis, roughly an hour from central Cairo depending on traffic.
  2. Memphis. The Colossus and the Alabaster Sphinx, with the Egyptologist's capital story.
  3. Saqqara. The Step Pyramid enclosure and one or two highlights.
  4. Lunch en route.
  5. Dahshur. The Bent Pyramid viewpoint, then the Red Pyramid.
  6. Back to Cairo.

The tour includes a licensed Egyptologist guide, transport, hotel pickup, lunch and entrance tickets. Travelling independently, you pay for a car and driver plus separate tickets (EGP 800, about €13, per adult for Saqqara and Dahshur alone, before Memphis), and manage the waits between sites. At €33 per seat, the shared tour is hard to beat. If you are travelling on a package such as Egypt in Depth, check its itinerary to see which of these sites it covers before adding this day.

Saqqara and Dahshur vs Giza: which one(s)?

The three sites are complements, not substitutes, but they cost time, so here is the comparison a planner actually needs.

Giza Saqqara Dahshur
What it shows The finished icon The prototype (Step Pyramid) The experiment and the fix
Roughly dated Khufu, about 2560 BC Djoser, about 2670 BC Sneferu, about 2600 BC
Crowds Egypt's busiest site Quiet Quietest of the three
Going inside Separately ticketed interiors Tombs and enclosure; Step Pyramid interior on its own ticket when open Red Pyramid included in the site ticket
Time needed Half a day Half a day (full site: more) 2 to 3 hours
Best for First visit, the icon The story, photography Quiet and pyramid interiors

Our ordering advice: see Giza first, because it is the reference point everything else plays against (our guide to the pyramids and the Grand Egyptian Museum in one day covers it), then take this loop when you want the story and the silence.

Saqqara and Dahshur are worth a day once Giza is planned: the prototype, the failed draft and the first true pyramid on one quiet loop south of Cairo, with ancient Memphis folded in on the road. faq.q: Are Saqqara and Dahshur worth visiting?
faq.a: Yes, if Giza is already on your list and you have a second day. Saqqara is older than Giza and far quieter, and Dahshur holds the Red Pyramid, the first true pyramid, whose interior is covered by the site ticket. As a single loop with Memphis it takes about 9 hours and is one of the cheapest full days out of Cairo, from €33 per person, as listed in November 2026.

As part of the loop, yes: the reclining Colossus of Ramesses II and the Alabaster Sphinx are genuinely striking, and Memphis sits on the route south. On its own it is thin, so bundle it with Saqqara and Dahshur rather than making it a dedicated trip.

faq.q: Can you go inside the Red Pyramid at Dahshur?
faq.a: Yes. The interior is covered by the Dahshur site ticket, with no extra charge of the kind Giza's pyramid interiors carry; on the tour, your guide advises on the day. Expect a steep, enclosed shaft and low chambers; skip it if you are claustrophobic or unsteady on stairs, and enjoy the view from the base instead.

faq.q: How long do Memphis, Saqqara and Dahshur need?
faq.a: One long day: about 9 hours door to door on the tour, with hotel pickup included. Independently, allow more, because waiting for drivers between the three sites adds up in the midday heat.

faq.q: Saqqara or Giza: which should you visit first?
faq.a: Giza first. It is the icon, and it gives you the reference point that makes Saqqara's prototype and Dahshur's experiments legible. The story lands better told forwards.
